summary:
Región de Coquimbo stands under Chile's national framework for trans people, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition under Gender Identity Law 21,120 has operated since 27 December 2019 on a self-determination basis for adults, with no therapy or surgery required; same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022; civil unions since 2015; birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006; and the Zamudio Law of 2012 has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences since 2018.

The Outright International Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, contains no Coquimbo-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding. What can be said about this region therefore rests on Chilean law as it applies nationwide and on the regional case counts published by Movilh.

The national policy direction has been restrictive for two years. In January 2025 the Constitutional Court annulled the section 46 provision of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents; in November 2025 Congress nonetheless defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombudsman for children. The Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres, and the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved, by 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding CEI 57 commission report recommending elimination of the Gender Identity Support Program, restrictions on minors' progressive autonomy, a ban on hormonal treatment for minors and repeal of the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) supplies division-specific figures from its national regional table. Coquimbo accounts for 2.62% of nationally documented abuse cases, a rise of 17.6% year-on-year in 2025. Nationally the report counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest in 24 years; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell, while the other 14 regions rose. The report reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate.
tangentialFactors:
Coquimbo's 17.6% year-on-year rise in documented abuse cases runs against the two largest regions, Valparaíso and Metropolitana, where recorded cases fell by 17.56% and 14.35% respectively. Movilh attributes the national pattern to hatred moving into regions with less public debate about sexual diversity and gender identity.

The 2024 Coquimbo share cited in comparisons does not appear in the 2025 edition of the Movilh report, so the trajectory rests on the 2025 figure and the reported year-on-year change rather than on a published series of shares.

Restrictive measures active at national level are proposals and budget decisions rather than binding rules on visitors: the CEI 57 report is explicitly non-binding, the Constitutional Court struck down the 2025 Budget Law restriction on financing hormone therapies, and the Ministry of Health-run support programme continues despite the defunding of the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program.
localsOnly:
Chilean residents may change registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery under Gender Identity Law 21,120. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, but that ruling applies only to that case.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Outright International Chile country dossier carries no division-specific information, so no Coquimbo-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding is available from that source. The regional reading in this record rests on Movilh's national regional table and on Chilean law as it applies nationwide.

The 2024 Coquimbo share of nationally documented abuse cases is not sourced: the 2025 Movilh edition does not publish it, and the comparison figure remains unresolved.

Whether the co-funding arrangements for trans-specific care in the Coquimbo health services differ from national arrangements is not sourced here.
